weighing.summary: The sources do not give one dead count; they give different counts. (1) Killed on the field, by the armies' returns: Union 3,155 (the revised return; the first return said 2,834) and Confederate 2,592 (the Official Records' compilation; Guild's own table 2,396); in both armies the mortally wounded stand with the wounded. (2) Killed or died of wounds: Union 5,291 (Fox, from the regimental rolls); for the Confederates no roll count exists, only estimates (Livermore 3,903, the plan's Busey and Martin 4,708) and Weaver's 1864 estimate of the rebel bodies buried on the field and at the hospitals, not less than 7,000. (3) Bodies taken up: Union 3,512 (Weaver). (4) The plan's totals of 8,000, 8,900 and 3,100 plus 4,700 have no source in the record. The Union figures differ because they count different things and are explained by it (settled in kind). The Confederate figures differ in what they count and also in size, and no source separates a count from an estimate: the best witnesses disagree and no rule in the rubric ranks them, so the conflict is irreducible and the default is a range per army.
weighing.who: Meade and Guild signed returns of their armies (relayed from corps returns). The Official Records' Confederate aggregate was compiled in 1889 by War Department editors, who call it approximative. Fox compiled the rolls of the Union regiments; Livermore computed; Weaver opened the graves and counted. Alexander, the Comte de Paris and the New York commission relay the returns.
weighing.when: Meade 1 Oct 1863, revised in the volume of 1889; Guild 1 Sep 1863; Weaver 19 Mar 1864; the Comte de Paris 1877; Fox 1889; Livermore 1900; the New York commission 1900; Alexander 1907; the Park Service 2018. By the rule a return or report of the time outranks a table compiled later (Guild's own return of Sep 1863 is the earlier document, but it leaves out the cavalry, so the editors' fuller aggregate is the low end of the range and Guild's 2,396 stays selectable); and a table of returns outranks a history; the records of the time (returns, Weaver) are therefore the ones carrying the range, and the later compilations are listed with what they count.
weighing.where: Weaver stood on the field for the five months of the disinterment and says how he knew; his count of bodies is a count of graves opened and Confederate burials he estimates. The returns of both armies were made from regimental reports, the Confederate one with no return from Jenkins' brigade and with the slightly wounded excluded (Lee's order of 14 May 1863, as the New York volume says), so it is known to be short. The Union return counts as killed only those killed or dying on the field.
weighing.how_knew: The Union return is a count from nominal lists; the Confederate return is the sum of commanders' reports, with the editors' caution. Fox's 5,291 is a name-by-name count of regimental rolls. Weaver's 7,000 is an estimate made "from time to time, as I went over the field". Livermore's 3,903 is computed from a ratio. The NPS 10,000 is rounded. Which digit Fox prints (5,291 or 5,091) was checked in three scans of his book and in his table, which sums to 5,291; the 5,091 of the New York volumes is not Fox's.
weighing.clock: not applicable: these are counts. The dates are the dates of the returns and reports.
weighing.independence: Groups: the Union return (Livermore, Alexander and the New York commission repeat it: one line), Meade's first return (with Halleck), Fox (rolls), Weaver, Guild, the Official Records' Confederate compilation (Alexander and Livermore repeat it), Livermore's estimate, the Comte de Paris, the Park Service. Each default end therefore rests on one line of knowledge and carries a single_source flag; no two independent counts of the same thing were found for the Confederate dead.

owner_note: DEC-008 consequence, reported and not edited: the man-by-man picture takes a unit's printed total and a procedural split of killed, wounded and missing from army-level fractions (casualty-sources.json). The killed fraction there is the killed-on-the-field fraction (Union 3,155 of 23,049 = 13.7 per cent; Confederate 13.9 to 20.3 per cent from the PDF sources). If the owner chooses the killed-or-died-of-wounds count for the Union (5,291), the fraction of those who lie dead would be about 23 per cent of the army loss, not 13.7; the Confederate Official Records return would give 12.7 per cent. No crowd count (one soldier per unit strength) changes, only the share of drawn men who fall dead rather than wounded.
